summary: Lithium carbonate is a mood-stabilizing agent indicated as monotherapy for bipolar I disorder (acute manic/mixed episodes and maintenance). It has a narrow therapeutic index with toxicity occurring at concentrations close to therapeutic levels, so frequent serum lithium monitoring is mandatory. Dehydration, salt restriction, renal impairment, and many drugs (diuretics, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors/ARBs) can precipitate toxicity.
indications: Bipolar I disorder - treatment of acute manic and mixed episodes (patients 7 years and older)
Bipolar I disorder - maintenance treatment (patients 7 years and older)

dosage.c: Maintenance treatment of bipolar I disorder
dosage.d: Adjust to maintain serum lithium 0.8-1.0 mEq/L
dosage.n: Use the lowest effective dose; monitor regularly

admin: Take with food to minimize GI upset
Maintain a consistent dietary salt and fluid intake; avoid dehydration
Swallow extended-release tablets whole - do not chew or crush
Obtain a serum lithium level after about 3 days, drawn 12 hours after the last dose, and regularly until stabilized
moa: The mechanism of action of lithium as a mood-stabilizing agent is unknown. It is thought to modulate intracellular second-messenger systems (including inhibition of inositol monophosphatase and glycogen synthase kinase-3) and to alter monoaminergic neurotransmission and neuronal signaling.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to any inactive ingredient in the lithium product
monitor: Serum lithium concentration (toxicity near therapeutic range)

preg: Lithium may cause harm in pregnancy. First-trimester use has been associated with cardiovascular malformations, especially Ebstein's anomaly (the increased risk is likely small). There is also concern for maternal and neonatal lithium toxicity during late pregnancy and the postpartum period; if used, monitor levels closely and reduce around delivery.
lact: Lithium is excreted in human breast milk and infant serum concentrations can be appreciable. Breastfeeding is generally not recommended; if used, monitor the infant for toxicity (hypotonia, lethargy, poor feeding) and renal/thyroid function.
renal: Lithium is renally cleared. In mild to moderate renal impairment (CLcr 30-89 mL/min) start below usual doses and titrate slowly with frequent monitoring; avoid lithium in severe renal impairment (CLcr <30 mL/min). Chronic therapy itself can cause kidney disease.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is required for hepatic impairment because lithium is not metabolized and is excreted unchanged by the kidneys.

major: Diuretics (especially thiazides) - reduce lithium clearance and raise levels (toxicity)
NSAIDs - reduce renal lithium clearance and raise levels
ACE inhibitors / ARBs - raise lithium levels
Metronidazole - raises lithium levels and renal toxicity
Serotonergic agents - increased serotonin syndrome risk
moderate: Antipsychotics (haloperidol and others) - neurologic reactions / encephalopathy
minor: Theophylline, caffeine, acetazolamide, high sodium intake (increase lithium clearance, lower levels)
interactions.food: Take with food; keep salt and fluid intake consistent - low sodium raises levels
interactions.alcohol: Avoid - dehydration can raise lithium levels
interactions.diagnostics: May affect thyroid function tests; monitor serum lithium, electrolytes, calcium, and renal function

serious: Lithium toxicity (coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion, vomiting, diarrhea)
emergency: Severe lithium toxicity (seizures, coma, irreversible brain damage)

monitoring: Serum lithium concentration (target 0.8-1.2 mEq/L acute; 0.8-1.0 mEq/L maintenance), drawn 12 hours post-dose
Renal function before and during therapy
Signs of toxicity, especially with dehydration, illness, or new interacting drugs
counsel: Take exactly as prescribed - the safe and toxic doses are very close
Maintain a steady intake of salt and fluids; avoid dehydration, heavy sweating, and low-salt diets
Report tremor, vomiting, diarrhea, drowsiness, slurred speech, or unsteadiness - these may signal toxicity
Do not start NSAIDs, water pills, or new medicines without checking with your prescriber
Attend regular blood tests for lithium level, kidney, and thyroid function
Tell your prescriber if you become ill, pregnant, or significantly change your diet
pk: Supports divided daily dosing to maintain target level
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); protect from moisture
pearls: Boxed warning: lithium toxicity occurs at concentrations close to therapeutic - serum level monitoring is mandatory
Dehydration, low salt, diuretics, NSAIDs, and ACE inhibitors/ARBs all raise levels and precipitate toxicity
Draw lithium levels 12 hours after the last dose for consistency
Monitor thyroid and renal function long-term; chronic use can cause CKD and hypothyroidism
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered unless it is nearly time for the next dose, in which case skip it and resume the usual schedule. Never double the dose - this can cause toxicity.
overdose: Toxic concentrations (>= 1.5 mEq/L) are close to therapeutic; at >3 mEq/L patients may progress to seizures, coma, and irreversible brain damage. There is no specific antidote. Mild toxicity may resolve with dose reduction or cessation; ensure hydration and correct sodium. Gastric lavage may be performed (activated charcoal does not bind lithium). Hemodialysis is the treatment of choice for severe toxicity, removing lithium rapidly and effectively. Contact a poison control center.
